claim: Proteasome inhibition with MG-132 (10 μM) for 2 hr led to a dramatic decrease in protein synthesis in cultured hippocampal neurons.
source: Blocking proteasome activity with either of two chemically distinct inhibitors (MG-132, 10 μM; Lactacystin, 10 μM; Figure 1A–E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–F) for 2 hr led to a dramatic decrease in protein synthesis, measured with two different labeling methods: the non-canonical amino acid azidohomoalanine (AHA) and BONCAT (biorthogonal non-canonical amino acid tagging) (Dieterich et al., 2006; Figure 1B–C) or metabolic labeling with puromycin (Figure 1D,E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data using BONCAT and puromycin labeling methods shown in Figure 1B-E.

claim: Proteasome inhibition with Lactacystin (10 μM) for 2 hr led to a dramatic decrease in protein synthesis in cultured hippocampal neurons.
source: Blocking proteasome activity with either of two chemically distinct inhibitors (MG-132, 10 μM; Lactacystin, 10 μM; Figure 1A–E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–F) for 2 hr led to a dramatic decrease in protein synthesis, measured with two different labeling methods: the non-canonical amino acid azidohomoalanine (AHA) and BONCAT (biorthogonal non-canonical amino acid tagging) (Dieterich et al., 2006; Figure 1B–C) or metabolic labeling with puromycin (Figure 1D,E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data using BONCAT and puromycin labeling methods shown in Figure 1.

claim: Dose-dependent reductions in proteasome activity led to coordinate reductions in protein synthesis.
source: The compensatory proteostatic decrease in protein synthesis did not require a complete block of proteasomal activity: dose-dependent reductions in proteasome activity led to coordinate reductions in protein synthesis (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D demonstrating dose-dependent effects.

claim: Cross-talk can occur between the protein degradation and synthesis pathways in response to relatively small fluctuations in proteasome activity.
source: These data suggest that cross-talk can occur between the protein degradation and synthesis pathways in response to relatively small fluctuations in proteasome activity.
evidence: Inferred from the dose-dependent relationship between proteasome activity and protein synthesis.

claim: Proteasome inhibition led to a decrease in protein synthesis apparent in both the cell bodies and dendrites of neurons.
source: In neurons, we observed that proteasome inhibition led to a decrease in protein synthesis apparent in both the cell bodies and dendrites of neurons (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by in situ puromycylation data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The reduction in protein synthesis following proteasome inhibition was not due to cell death.
source: The reduction in protein synthesis was not due to cell death (Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A) or compromised cell health as protein synthesis levels were restored following an extensive (14 hr) washout of the proteasome inhibitor (Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 2B–D).
evidence: Supported by cell viability assays and washout experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A-D.

claim: Protein synthesis levels were restored following an extensive (14 hr) washout of the proteasome inhibitor.
source: The reduction in protein synthesis was not due to cell death (Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A) or compromised cell health as protein synthesis levels were restored following an extensive (14 hr) washout of the proteasome inhibitor (Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 2B–D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B-D.

claim: Overexpression of a mutant ubiquitin molecule, K48R+G76A, decreased protein synthesis.
source: Furthermore, the overexpression of a mutant ubiquitin molecule, K48R+G76A (which inhibits polyubiquitination and is resistant to deubiquitinases thus inhibiting protein degradation by the proteasome [Hodgins et al., 1992; Ju and Xie, 2004; Ju and Xie, 2006] also decreased protein synthesis (Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 2,E–F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 2E-F, with citations to prior work on this mutant.

claim: The mutant ubiquitin K48R+G76A inhibits polyubiquitination and is resistant to deubiquitinases thus inhibiting protein degradation by the proteasome.
source: Furthermore, the overexpression of a mutant ubiquitin molecule, K48R+G76A (which inhibits polyubiquitination and is resistant to deubiquitinases thus inhibiting protein degradation by the proteasome [Hodgins et al., 1992; Ju and Xie, 2004; Ju and Xie, 2006] also decreased protein synthesis (Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 2,E–F).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Hodgins et al., 1992; Ju and Xie, 2004; Ju and Xie, 2006).

claim: Protein synthesis in neurites was significantly inhibited by proteasome inhibition.
source: We found that protein synthesis in neurites was also significantly inhibited by proteasome inhibition (Figure 1I,J), indicating that the feedback mechanism coupling protein degradation to synthesis also functions locally in neuronal processes.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from isolated dendrites/axons shown in Figure 1I,J.

claim: The feedback mechanism coupling protein degradation to synthesis functions locally in neuronal processes.
source: We found that protein synthesis in neurites was also significantly inhibited by proteasome inhibition (Figure 1I,J), indicating that the feedback mechanism coupling protein degradation to synthesis also functions locally in neuronal processes.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that protein synthesis in isolated neurites is inhibited by proteasome inhibition.

claim: Blocking transcription during proteasome inhibition did not affect the reduction in protein synthesis.
source: To determine the mechanisms by which protein synthesis is reduced, we first asked whether proteasome inhibition brings about a reduction in protein synthesis by altering transcription. Blocking transcription during proteasome inhibition, however, did not affect the reduction in protein synthesis we previously observed (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data using actinomycin D shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: Proteasome inhibition did not change the free amino acid content of neurons.
source: Because proteasome activity can contribute to amino acid recycling in cells, we measured the free amino acid content of the neurons, and we did not find any changes following proteasome inhibition (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by amino acid measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The translation factors eIF4B, eIF4EBP1/2, and eIF4G showed no change in phosphorylation following proteasome inhibition.
source: The translation factors eIF4B, eIF4EBP1/2, and eIF4G showed no change in phosphorylation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D–E).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D-E.

claim: A marked and rapid increase in the phosphorylation of eIF2α was observed following proteasome inhibition, without a change in total eIF2α levels.
source: In contrast, as has been observed in mouse embryonic fibroblasts and other cell types (Fribley et al., 2004; Jiang and Wek, 2005; Mazroui et al., 2007; Nawrocki et al., 2005; Vabulas and Hartl, 2005; Yerlikaya et al., 2008; Zhang et al., 2010), we observed a marked and rapid increase in the phosphorylation of eIF2α (a key regulator of translation initiation) (Harding et al., 2000), without a change in total eIF2α levels (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2A-C and citations to prior work in other cell types.

claim: eIF2α is a key regulator of translation initiation.
source: In contrast, as has been observed in mouse embryonic fibroblasts and other cell types (Fribley et al., 2004; Jiang and Wek, 2005; Mazroui et al., 2007; Nawrocki et al., 2005; Vabulas and Hartl, 2005; Yerlikaya et al., 2008; Zhang et al., 2010), we observed a marked and rapid increase in the phosphorylation of eIF2α (a key regulator of translation initiation) (Harding et al., 2000), without a change in total eIF2α levels (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: Supported by citation to Harding et al., 2000.

claim: Treatment with ISRIB reversed the effects of proteasomal inhibition on protein synthesis.
source: Consistent with a causal role of eIF2α phosphorylation in the inhibition of neuronal protein synthesis, we found that treatment with the integrated stress response inhibitor (that acts downstream of peIF2α) (ISRIB; [Sidrauski et al., 2015]) reversed the effects of proteasomal inhibition on protein synthesis (Figure 2D,E), without affecting basal levels of translation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D,E and citation to Sidrauski et al., 2015.

claim: ISRIB acts downstream of peIF2α.
source: Consistent with a causal role of eIF2α phosphorylation in the inhibition of neuronal protein synthesis, we found that treatment with the integrated stress response inhibitor (that acts downstream of peIF2α) (ISRIB; [Sidrauski et al., 2015]) reversed the effects of proteasomal inhibition on protein synthesis (Figure 2D,E), without affecting basal levels of translation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sidrauski et al., 2015.

claim: ISRIB did not affect basal levels of translation.
source: Consistent with a causal role of eIF2α phosphorylation in the inhibition of neuronal protein synthesis, we found that treatment with the integrated stress response inhibitor (that acts downstream of peIF2α) (ISRIB; [Sidrauski et al., 2015]) reversed the effects of proteasomal inhibition on protein synthesis (Figure 2D,E), without affecting basal levels of translation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1F.

claim: There are four kinases known to phosphorylate eIF2α: PERK, PKR, GCN2, and HRI.
source: There are four kinases that are known to phosphorylate eIF2α, the eIF2α kinases 1–4, commonly known as PERK (PKR-like ER kinase), PKR (protein kinase double-stranded RNA-dependent), GCN2 (general control non-derepressible-2), and HRI (heme-regulated inhibitor) (Donnelly et al., 2013; Taniuchi et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Donnelly et al., 2013 and Taniuchi et al., 2016.

claim: GCN2 is a regulator of translation in neurons during synaptic plasticity.
source: In order to evaluate which kinase (or kinases) phosphorylates eIF2α in response to proteasome inhibition, we first focused on GCN2 since it is well-established as a regulator of translation in neurons during synaptic plasticity (Costa-Mattioli et al., 2005; Trinh and Klann, 2013), and was previously described to be activated in response to proteasome inhibitors in D. melanogaster (Suraweera et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Costa-Mattioli et al., 2005 and Trinh and Klann, 2013.

claim: GCN2 was previously described to be activated in response to proteasome inhibitors in D. melanogaster.
source: In order to evaluate which kinase (or kinases) phosphorylates eIF2α in response to proteasome inhibition, we first focused on GCN2 since it is well-established as a regulator of translation in neurons during synaptic plasticity (Costa-Mattioli et al., 2005; Trinh and Klann, 2013), and was previously described to be activated in response to proteasome inhibitors in D. melanogaster (Suraweera et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Suraweera et al., 2012.

claim: In the absence of GCN2, protein synthesis was still inhibited by proteasome blockade.
source: Using cultured neurons from GCN2 knock-out mice we examined the sensitivity of protein synthesis to proteasomal inhibition. Surprisingly, in the absence of GCN2 protein synthesis was still inhibited by proteasome blockade (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from GCN2 KO neurons shown in Figure 3A.

claim: In the absence of PERK, protein synthesis was still inhibited by proteasome blockade.
source: We conducted the same experiments in cultured neurons obtained from PERK knock-out mice or in PKR-inhibited neurons and again observed no effect on the proteasome-dependent inhibition of protein synthesis (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from PERK KO neurons shown in Figure 3A.

claim: In PKR-inhibited neurons, protein synthesis was still inhibited by proteasome blockade.
source: We conducted the same experiments in cultured neurons obtained from PERK knock-out mice or in PKR-inhibited neurons and again observed no effect on the proteasome-dependent inhibition of protein synthesis (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from PKR-inhibited neurons shown in Figure 3A.

claim: HRI is primarily activated by reduced cellular heme levels and plays an important role in regulating globin translation in erythrocytes.
source: We thus turned our attention to the least likely candidate, HRI, a kinase that is primarily activated by reduced cellular heme levels and is known to play an important role in regulating globin translation in erythrocytes (Han et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to Han et al., 2001.

claim: In neurons from HRI knock-out mice, there was a dramatically reduced inhibition of protein synthesis induced by proteasome blockade.
source: Using neurons from an HRI knock-out mouse (Han et al., 2001) we observed a dramatically reduced inhibition of protein synthesis induced by proteasome blockade with metabolic labeling detected by western blot (Figure 3B,C) or in situ labeling of cultured hippocampal neurons (Figure 3D,E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from HRI KO neurons shown in Figure 3B-E and citation to Han et al., 2001.

claim: HRI deletion had no effect on the basal levels of protein synthesis in neurons or in brain tissue.
source: HRI deletion had no effect on the basal levels of protein synthesis in neurons or in brain tissue (Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: The absence of HRI significantly reduced the proteasome inhibition-induced increase in eIF2α phosphorylation.
source: The absence of HRI also significantly reduced the proteasome inhibition-induced increase in eIF2α phosphorylation (Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), while the absence or inhibition of the other eIF2α kinases did not (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The absence or inhibition of GCN2, PERK, or PKR did not reduce the proteasome inhibition-induced increase in eIF2α phosphorylation.
source: The absence of HRI also significantly reduced the proteasome inhibition-induced increase in eIF2α phosphorylation (Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), while the absence or inhibition of the other eIF2α kinases did not (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D,E.

claim: HRI transcript is the most abundant of the 4 eIF2α kinases in hippocampal neurons.
source: Using data from a recent RNA-sequencing study (Tushev et al., 2018) we found that the HRI transcript is the most abundant of the 4 eIF2α kinases (Figure 3G) in hippocampal neurons.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3G and citation to Tushev et al., 2018.

claim: HRI mRNA is detected in both somata and dendrites of hippocampal neurons.
source: We used fluorescence in situ hybridization to validate and localize HRI mRNA in hippocampal neurons and tissue, and detected it in both somata and dendrites (Figure 3H and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–D).
evidence: Supported by FISH data shown in Figure 3H and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A-D.

claim: HRI expression level in brain was very low compared to the HRI levels detected in heme-rich tissues like liver or blood.
source: We observed that the HRI expression level in brain was very low compared to the HRI levels detected in heme-rich tissues like liver or blood (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: Proteasome inhibition did not change HRI mRNA levels.
source: Quantification of HRI mRNA using droplet digital PCR (ddPCR) revealed no change in HRI mRNA levels following 2 hr of proteasome inhibition (Figure 4A), consistent with the transcription-independence of the protein synthesis reduction elicited by proteasome inhibition (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by ddPCR data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Following treatment with a proteasome inhibitor for 2 hr there was a significant upregulation in neuronal HRI protein levels.
source: Following treatment with a proteasome inhibitor for 2 hr there was, however, a significant upregulation in neuronal HRI protein levels (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1D), suggesting that HRI might be a proteasome substrate.
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: HRI was degraded by the proteasome in an in vitro assay with purified 20S proteasome and recombinant HRI.
source: Although we were unable to detect appreciable polyubiquitylation of HRI (data not shown), using an in vitro assay with purified 20S proteasome and recombinant HRI we observed that HRI was degraded by the proteasome (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E,F).
evidence: Supported by in vitro degradation assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E,F.

claim: HRI protein has an extremely short half-life under control conditions (~4.2 hr).
source: To estimate the magnitude of this effect, we metabolically pulse-labeled cultured neurons with S35Methionine and immunoprecipitated HRI at different chase times under control and proteasome inhibition conditions. Surprisingly, we observed that HRI protein has an extremely short half-life under control conditions (~4.2 hr).
evidence: Supported by pulse-chase experiment data shown in Figure 4C,D.

claim: The short-lived HRI protein was significantly stabilized by proteasome inhibition.
source: In addition, the short-lived HRI protein was significantly stabilized by proteasome inhibition (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: Supported by pulse-chase experiment data shown in Figure 4C,D.

claim: Transfection of a bi-directional plasmid with ZsGreen and HA-tagged HRI into neurons followed by DOX treatment led to robust expression of ZsGreen but barely detectable expression of HRI in the same population.
source: Transfection of the plasmid into neurons or HeLa cells followed by DOX treatment led to robust expression of ZsGreen in a large population of cells whereas the expression of HRI was absent or barely detectable in the same population (Figure 4F,G and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: Supported by transfection experiment data shown in Figure 4F,G and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A-C.

claim: Following proteasome inhibition, there was a leftward shift in the translational profile from polysomes to monosomes.
source: As shown in Figure 5A and consistent with the relative inhibition of translation observed in Figure 1, we observed a leftward shift in the translational profile from polysomes to monosomes following proteasome inhibition.
evidence: Supported by polysome profiling data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Beta-actin mRNA exhibited a leftward shift to the monosome fraction after proteasome inhibition.
source: We confirmed this shift using ddPCR to detect beta-actin mRNA levels in each fraction in control and PI conditions (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by ddPCR data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: HRI mRNA exhibited a paradoxical rightward shift to the polysomal fractions following proteasome inhibition.
source: In contrast, HRI mRNA did not exhibit a leftward shift after proteasome inhibition, but rather exhibited a paradoxical rightward shift to the polysomal fractions (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by ddPCR data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: HRI has a very short 5'UTR and no uORF or IRES is predicted.
source: HRI, however, has a very short 5'UTR and no uORF or IRES is predicted (Di Prisco et al., 2014; Mokrejs et al., 2010; Wu et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Di Prisco et al., 2014; Mokrejs et al., 2010; Wu et al., 2009.

claim: HRI mRNA possesses many rare and extremely rare codons.
source: We evaluated the rodent HRI sequence for the presence of rare codons and found a number of rare and extremely rare codons, HRI uses more rare codons than 86.78% of the genes expressed in the hippocampus (see Materials and methods), predicting compromised translation (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by codon usage analysis shown in Figure 5D and Materials and methods.

claim: HRI uses more rare codons than 86.78% of the genes expressed in the hippocampus.
source: We evaluated the rodent HRI sequence for the presence of rare codons and found a number of rare and extremely rare codons, HRI uses more rare codons than 86.78% of the genes expressed in the hippocampus (see Materials and methods), predicting compromised translation (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by codon adaptation index analysis described in Materials and methods.

claim: Expression of an HA-tagged HRI with optimized codon usage (HRIopt-HA) resulted in higher basal expression than wild-type HRI.
source: Indeed, when we expressed an HA-tagged HRI with optimized codon usage (HRIopt-HA) we observed that the basal expression of HRIopt-HA was higher (Figure 5E,G and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B) and HRIopt-HA exhibited a reduced rightward shift to the polysome fraction following treatment with a proteasome inhibitor (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by transfection and imaging data shown in Figure 5E,G and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: HRIopt-HA exhibited a reduced rightward shift to the polysome fraction following treatment with a proteasome inhibitor.
source: Indeed, when we expressed an HA-tagged HRI with optimized codon usage (HRIopt-HA) we observed that the basal expression of HRIopt-HA was higher (Figure 5E,G and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B) and HRIopt-HA exhibited a reduced rightward shift to the polysome fraction following treatment with a proteasome inhibitor (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by polysome profiling data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: HRI protein expression is paradoxically enhanced under conditions in which global protein synthesis is reduced.
source: Taken together these data indicate that HRI protein expression is paradoxically enhanced under conditions in which global protein synthesis is reduced.
evidence: Inferred from the combination of HRI stabilization and enhanced translation during proteasome inhibition.

claim: Two complementary mechanisms act to enhance HRI levels: stabilization of the protein via reduced degradation by the proteasome and enhanced translation owing to the increased availability of rare codons.
source: Two complementary mechanisms act to enhance HRI levels; first, a stabilization of the protein via reduced degradation by the proteasome and, second, enhanced translation owing to the increased availability of rare codons.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental data on HRI degradation and codon usage.

claim: In erythrocyte precursors, HRI kinase is activated by multiple mechanisms, including an increase in reactive oxygen species (ROS) or nitric oxide (NO) or reductions in cellular heme.
source: In erythrocyte precursors, HRI kinase is activated by multiple mechanisms, including an increase in reactive oxygen species (ROS) or nitric oxide (NO) or reductions in cellular heme (Chen, 2000; Chen and London, 1995; Chen et al., 1991; Igarashi et al., 2004; Uma et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chen, 2000; Chen and London, 1995; Chen et al., 1991; Igarashi et al., 2004; Uma et al., 2001.

claim: Increases in ROS have been reported following proteasome inhibition.
source: Increases in ROS have been reported following proteasome inhibition (Ding et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ding et al., 2006.

claim: Neither ROS scavengers nor NO synthase inhibitors prevented the proteasome inhibitor-induced decreases in protein synthesis.
source: We thus tested whether the HRI activation that follows proteasome inhibition is due to increases in either ROS or NO by quenching ROS or blocking NO synthesis during MG132 treatment. We found that neither ROS scavengers nor NO synthase inhibitors prevented the proteasome inhibitor-induced decreases in protein synthesis (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A-E.

claim: Treatment with heme oxygenase inhibitors failed to affect the protein synthesis reduction elicited by proteasome inhibition.
source: Treatment with two different heme oxygenase inhibitors, however, also failed to affect the protein synthesis reduction elicited by proteasome inhibition (Figure 5—figure supplement 2F,G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2F,G.

claim: Enhanced heme breakdown is not responsible for HRI activation following proteasome inhibition.
source: These data suggest that enhanced heme breakdown, per se, is not responsible for HRI activation.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of effect of heme oxygenase inhibitors on protein synthesis reduction.

claim: Blood had high levels of free heme while heme could not be detected in cultured hippocampal neurons.
source: We directly measured free heme in neurons and blood and found that while blood had predictably high levels of free heme, heme could not even be detected in cultured hippocampal neurons, and total hippocampal lysates exhibited heme levels orders of magnitude lower than blood (hippocampus; 36 ± 8 fmol/μg, blood; 126 ± 18 pmol/μg).
evidence: Supported by direct heme measurements in neurons and blood.

claim: Total hippocampal lysates exhibited heme levels orders of magnitude lower than blood (hippocampus; 36 ± 8 fmol/μg, blood; 126 ± 18 pmol/μg).
source: We directly measured free heme in neurons and blood and found that while blood had predictably high levels of free heme, heme could not even be detected in cultured hippocampal neurons, and total hippocampal lysates exhibited heme levels orders of magnitude lower than blood (hippocampus; 36 ± 8 fmol/μg, blood; 126 ± 18 pmol/μg).
evidence: Supported by direct heme measurements.

claim: The addition of hemin led to a significant reduction in eIF2α phosphorylation by HRI in an in vitro assay.
source: We next tested if the measured amount of heme in blood could indeed inhibit HRI kinase activity in an in vitro assay using recombinant HRI and its substrate eIF2α, together with 32P-ATP. We found that the addition of hemin (heme complexed with Fe3+) led to a significant reduction in eIF2α phosphorylation by HRI (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by in vitro kinase assay data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: eIF2α phosphorylation was elevated in hippocampus when compared to blood in an in vitro assay with recombinant HRI and eIF2α added to cellular lysates.
source: Given the clear heme-induced inhibition of HRI, we directly tested whether the cytoplasmic regulatory context for HRI is different in neurons by adding recombinant HRI and its substrate eIF2α, together with 32P-ATP to cellular lysates prepared from neurons or blood. We evaluated the phosphorylation of eIF2α and found that it was elevated in hippocampus when compared to blood, indicating that HRI is more active under basal conditions in the neuronal cytoplasmic context (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by in vitro kinase assay data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: HRI is more active under basal conditions in the neuronal cytoplasmic context compared to blood.
source: Given the clear heme-induced inhibition of HRI, we directly tested whether the cytoplasmic regulatory context for HRI is different in neurons by adding recombinant HRI and its substrate eIF2α, together with 32P-ATP to cellular lysates prepared from neurons or blood. We evaluated the phosphorylation of eIF2α and found that it was elevated in hippocampus when compared to blood, indicating that HRI is more active under basal conditions in the neuronal cytoplasmic context (Figure 6B).
evidence: Inferred from the elevated eIF2α phosphorylation in hippocampal lysates compared to blood lysates.

claim: Addition of hemin to cultured neurons resulted in a rescue of the protein synthesis inhibition caused by proteasome blockade.
source: If the elevated HRI protein is constitutively active due to low neuronal heme levels, then the inhibition of protein synthesis induced by proteasome blockade should be amenable to rescue by exogenous heme in neurons. Indeed, we found that addition of hemin to cultured neurons resulted in a rescue of the protein synthesis inhibition (Figure 6C, Figure 5—figure supplement 2H), and a reduction in the phosphorylation levels of eIF2α (Figure 5—figure supplement 2I,J) caused by proteasome blockade.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C and Figure 5—figure supplement 2H.

claim: Addition of hemin to cultured neurons resulted in a reduction in the phosphorylation levels of eIF2α caused by proteasome blockade.
source: If the elevated HRI protein is constitutively active due to low neuronal heme levels, then the inhibition of protein synthesis induced by proteasome blockade should be amenable to rescue by exogenous heme in neurons. Indeed, we found that addition of hemin to cultured neurons resulted in a rescue of the protein synthesis inhibition (Figure 6C, Figure 5—figure supplement 2H), and a reduction in the phosphorylation levels of eIF2α (Figure 5—figure supplement 2I,J) caused by proteasome blockade.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2I,J.

claim: The addition of Hemin to HRI k.o. primary neurons had no effect on basal protein synthesis.
source: The addition of Hemin to HRI k.o. primary neurons had no effect on basal protein synthesis, ruling out an off-target effect of hemin (Figure 5—figure supplement 2K,L).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2K,L.

claim: Relatively low cytoplasmic heme levels in neurons favor the constitutive activity of HRI.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that relatively low cytoplasmic heme levels in neurons favor the constitutive activity of HRI.
evidence: Inferred from the combination of low heme levels in neurons, elevated HRI activity in neuronal lysates, and rescue by hemin.

claim: In neurons, the cytoplasmic environment is permissive for the constitutive activity of HRI upon expression.
source: This indicates that, in neurons, the cytoplasmic environment is permissive for the constitutive activity of HRI upon expression.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that neurons expressing HRI exhibit reduced protein synthesis.

claim: The small neuronal population that expressed appreciable levels of HRI exhibited significantly reduced protein synthesis relative to cells that did not express HRI.
source: We revisited the HRI over-expression experiments to examine protein synthesis in neurons expressing HRI or not. Brief metabolic labeling of transfected neurons to measure protein synthesis indicated that the small neuronal population that expressed appreciable levels of HRI exhibited significantly reduced protein synthesis, on average, relative to other cells that did not express HRI (Figure 6D,E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D,E.

claim: Small increases in HRI expression can have a significant impact on protein synthesis.
source: Furthermore, small increases in HRI expression can have a significant impact on protein synthesis (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: HRI's potent effect on global translation provides an explanation for why its expression is usually maintained at low levels in neurons.
source: In addition, HRI's potent effect on global translation provides an explanation for why its expression is usually maintained at low levels in neurons.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that HRI expression strongly inhibits protein synthesis.

claim: HRI's basal very low expression, short half-life and boost in protein levels upon proteasome inhibition make it both an optimal sensor and effector for proteostasis during situations of compromised proteasome activity.
source: These features of HRI, its basal very low expression, its short half-life and the boost in protein levels upon proteasome inhibition, thus make it both an optimal sensor and effector for proteostasis during situations of compromised proteasome activity.
evidence: Inferred from the combination of HRI's properties described in the manuscript.

claim: Proteasome inhibition stabilizes the extremely short-lived neuronal HRI protein.
source: Taken together, our data indicate the following sequence of events unfolds to restore proteostasis: i) proteasome inhibition (PI) stabilizes the extremely short-lived neuronal HRI protein, ii) endogenous low levels of neuronal heme result in constitutive activation of HRI which increases the phosphorylation of eIF2α and reduces translation initiation, iii) the initial decrease in general translation may lead to an increase in the availability of charged rare tRNAs (Saikia et al., 2016), further increasing the translation of HRI mRNA and ensuring ongoing phosphorylation of eIF2α and as a result, reduced global translation.
evidence: Supported by experimental data on HRI half-life and stabilization by proteasome inhibition.

claim: Endogenous low levels of neuronal heme result in constitutive activation of HRI which increases the phosphorylation of eIF2α and reduces translation initiation.
source: Taken together, our data indicate the following sequence of events unfolds to restore proteostasis: i) proteasome inhibition (PI) stabilizes the extremely short-lived neuronal HRI protein, ii) endogenous low levels of neuronal heme result in constitutive activation of HRI which increases the phosphorylation of eIF2α and reduces translation initiation, iii) the initial decrease in general translation may lead to an increase in the availability of charged rare tRNAs (Saikia et al., 2016), further increasing the translation of HRI mRNA and ensuring ongoing phosphorylation of eIF2α and as a result, reduced global translation.
evidence: Supported by experimental data on heme levels, HRI activity, and eIF2α phosphorylation.

claim: The initial decrease in general translation may lead to an increase in the availability of charged rare tRNAs, further increasing the translation of HRI mRNA.
source: Taken together, our data indicate the following sequence of events unfolds to restore proteostasis: i) proteasome inhibition (PI) stabilizes the extremely short-lived neuronal HRI protein, ii) endogenous low levels of neuronal heme result in constitutive activation of HRI which increases the phosphorylation of eIF2α and reduces translation initiation, iii) the initial decrease in general translation may lead to an increase in the availability of charged rare tRNAs (Saikia et al., 2016), further increasing the translation of HRI mRNA and ensuring ongoing phosphorylation of eIF2α and as a result, reduced global translation.
evidence: Speculative mechanism supported by citation to Saikia et al., 2016 and inference from experimental data.

claim: The feedback mechanism allows for the coordination of protein synthesis and degradation in neurons, so that global protein levels stay balanced.
source: The above-described mechanism allows for the coordination of protein synthesis and degradation in neurons, so that global protein levels stay balanced.
evidence: Inferred from the overall experimental findings.

claim: The same feedback mechanism can be detected in isolated neuronal processes, including dendrites and potentially axons.
source: We found that the same feedback mechanism can be detected in isolated neuronal processes, including dendrites and potentially axons.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from isolated neurites.

claim: Local synthesis and degradation of proteins occurs in dendrites and axons via localized mRNAs, ribosomes and components of the UPS.
source: Local synthesis and degradation of proteins occurs in dendrites and axons via localized mRNAs, ribosomes and components of the UPS (e.g. [Bingol and Schuman, 2006; Campbell and Holt, 2001; Hafner et al., 2019; Holt and Schuman, 2013]).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Bingol and Schuman, 2006; Campbell and Holt, 2001; Hafner et al., 2019; Holt and Schuman, 2013).

claim: While the HRI transcript is detected at higher levels than the other 3 eIF2α kinases in hippocampal neurons, the HRI protein is expressed at very low levels under basal conditions.
source: In this regard, it is interesting to note that while the HRI transcript is detected at higher levels than the other 3 eIF2α kinases in hippocampal neurons, the HRI protein is expressed at very low levels under basal conditions, suggesting strong cellular pressure to keep HRI protein expression low.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq and protein expression data.

claim: There is strong cellular pressure to keep HRI protein expression low.
source: In this regard, it is interesting to note that while the HRI transcript is detected at higher levels than the other 3 eIF2α kinases in hippocampal neurons, the HRI protein is expressed at very low levels under basal conditions, suggesting strong cellular pressure to keep HRI protein expression low.
evidence: Inferred from the discrepancy between high mRNA levels and low protein levels.

claim: HRI levels exhibit an increase upon proteasome inhibition, consistent with the observation that HRI can be degraded by the proteasome in vivo and in vitro.
source: We observed, though, that HRI levels exhibit an increase upon proteasome inhibition, consistent with our observation that HRI can be degraded by the proteasome in vivo and in vitro.
evidence: Supported by experimental data on HRI protein levels and degradation.

claim: Expression of a codon-optimized HRI resulted in higher levels of basal translation.
source: Indeed, HRI mRNA possesses many rare and extremely rare codons; expression of a codon-optimized HRI resulted in higher levels of basal translation.
evidence: Supported by experimental data on codon-optimized HRI expression.

claim: In polysome profiling experiments, HRI mRNA exhibited a paradoxical shift to the polysome fraction following proteasomal inhibition, while the bulk of cellular mRNAs exhibited a shift to the monosome fraction.
source: In addition, in polysome profiling experiments, we found that HRI mRNA exhibited a paradoxical shift to the polysome fraction following proteasomal inhibition, while the bulk of cellular mRNAs exhibited a shift to the monosome fraction, consistent with their reduced global translation.
evidence: Supported by polysome profiling data.

claim: Rare codon availability could explain the atypical behavior of HRI mRNA following PI.
source: Owing to the apparent absence of uORFs in the 5'UTR of HRI, we propose that rare codon availability could explain the atypical behavior of HRI mRNA following PI (Saikia et al., 2016), in support of this idea, the codon-optimized HRI failed to exhibit the shift to the polysome fraction upon PI.
evidence: Proposed mechanism supported by citation to Saikia et al., 2016 and experimental data on codon-optimized HRI.

claim: The codon-optimized HRI failed to exhibit the shift to the polysome fraction upon PI.
source: Owing to the apparent absence of uORFs in the 5'UTR of HRI, we propose that rare codon availability could explain the atypical behavior of HRI mRNA following PI (Saikia et al., 2016), in support of this idea, the codon-optimized HRI failed to exhibit the shift to the polysome fraction upon PI.
evidence: Supported by polysome profiling data on codon-optimized HRI.

claim: In erythrocytes, HRI is activated by reduced heme levels to coordinately reduce the synthesis of α- and β-globin.
source: In erythrocytes, HRI is activated by reduced heme levels to coordinately reduce the synthesis of α- and β-globin (Han et al., 2001); together α-globin, β-globin, and heme, assembled in a 2:2:4 ratio, make up hemoglobin.
evidence: Supported by citation to Han et al., 2001.

claim: α-globin, β-globin, and heme, assembled in a 2:2:4 ratio, make up hemoglobin.
source: In erythrocytes, HRI is activated by reduced heme levels to coordinately reduce the synthesis of α- and β-globin (Han et al., 2001); together α-globin, β-globin, and heme, assembled in a 2:2:4 ratio, make up hemoglobin.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge.

claim: Getting the stoichiometry just right is important for red blood cells since an overabundance of any single component is cytotoxic to RBCs and their precursors.
source: Getting the stoichiometry just right is important for red blood cells (RBCs) since an overabundance of any single component is cytotoxic to RBCs and their precursors.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about hemoglobin stoichiometry.

claim: Heme levels are extremely low or undetectable in neurons.
source: We found that heme levels are extremely low or undetectable in neurons, indicating that once expressed at appreciable levels, HRI will be constitutively active.
evidence: Supported by direct heme measurements in neurons.

claim: Once expressed at appreciable levels, HRI will be constitutively active in neurons.
source: We found that heme levels are extremely low or undetectable in neurons, indicating that once expressed at appreciable levels, HRI will be constitutively active.
evidence: Inferred from low heme levels and HRI's heme-dependent regulation.

claim: Significantly elevated HRI activity was observed in a control hippocampal lysate when compared to a control blood lysate.
source: Indeed, we observed significantly elevated HRI activity in a control hippocampal lysate when compared to a control blood lysate.
evidence: Supported by in vitro kinase assay data.

claim: The PI-induced protein synthesis inhibition was rescued by the addition of hemin.
source: Importantly and definitively, we observed that the PI-induced protein synthesis inhibition was rescued by the addition of hemin.
evidence: Supported by experimental data on hemin rescue.

claim: Under control conditions HRI exhibits barely detectable levels of expression and activity due to its high turn-over and low translation rates.
source: Taken together, multiple mechanisms act in concert to tightly control the dynamic range of HRI. Under control conditions HRI exhibits barely detectable levels of expression and activity due to its high turn-over and low translation rates.
evidence: Supported by experimental data on HRI half-life and translation.

claim: The inhibition of the proteasome is sensed by the stabilization of HRI.
source: The inhibition of the proteasome is sensed by the stabilization of HRI and the low neuronal heme content means that HRI can respond immediately to the environment created by proteasome blockade.
evidence: Supported by experimental data on HRI stabilization upon proteasome inhibition.

claim: The low neuronal heme content means that HRI can respond immediately to the environment created by proteasome blockade.
source: The inhibition of the proteasome is sensed by the stabilization of HRI and the low neuronal heme content means that HRI can respond immediately to the environment created by proteasome blockade.
evidence: Inferred from low heme levels and HRI's constitutive activity in neurons.

claim: Physiological and pathophysiological conditions that give rise to proteasome dysfunction may favor HRI expression and activity leading to a decrease in protein synthesis.
source: These data further suggest that physiological and pathophysiological conditions that give rise to proteasome dysfunction may favor HRI expression and activity leading to a decrease in protein synthesis.
evidence: Speculative extrapolation from experimental findings.

claim: All four of the eIF2α kinases have been associated with the phosphorylation of eIF2α in response to proteasome inhibition in cell lines of non-neuronal origin or mouse embryonic fibroblasts.
source: Indeed, all four of the eIF2α kinases have been associated with the phosphorylation of eIF2α in response to proteasome inhibition. These studies were performed with cell lines of non-neuronal origin or mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEF) (Jiang and Wek, 2005; Yerlikaya et al., 2008; Zhang et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Jiang and Wek, 2005; Yerlikaya et al., 2008; Zhang et al., 2010.

claim: The activation of mTOR pathway following UPS inhibition has been linked to a decrease in protein synthesis.
source: In addition, the activation of mTOR pathway following UPS inhibition has also been linked to a decrease in protein synthesis (Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2014.

claim: HRI is clearly the major kinase responsible for the proteasome inhibition-induced feedback regulation of neuronal protein synthesis.
source: In our experiments, HRI is clearly the major kinase responsible for the proteasome inhibition-induced feedback regulation of neuronal protein synthesis; we think it is likely, however, that the other eIF2α kinases also play a role, potentially when HRI is absent or during periods of prolonged proteasome inhibition.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from HRI KO neurons.

claim: The other eIF2α kinases likely also play a role in proteasome inhibition-induced feedback regulation, potentially when HRI is absent or during periods of prolonged proteasome inhibition.
source: In our experiments, HRI is clearly the major kinase responsible for the proteasome inhibition-induced feedback regulation of neuronal protein synthesis; we think it is likely, however, that the other eIF2α kinases also play a role, potentially when HRI is absent or during periods of prolonged proteasome inhibition.
evidence: Speculative statement based on incomplete rescue in HRI KO.

claim: HRI influences the translation of synaptic proteins.
source: We note that HRI's role in neuronal function is poorly explored, save for two reports of HRI influencing the translation of synaptic proteins (Ramos-Fernández et al., 2016) and influencing learning (ILL-Raga et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ramos-Fernández et al., 2016.

claim: HRI influences learning.
source: We note that HRI's role in neuronal function is poorly explored, save for two reports of HRI influencing the translation of synaptic proteins (Ramos-Fernández et al., 2016) and influencing learning (ILL-Raga et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to ILL-Raga et al., 2013.

claim: Emerging data point to dysregulation of iron homeostasis in disease.
source: In addition, the regulation by heme highlights an important element to consider in the context of neuronal function, given emerging data that point to dysregulation of iron homeostasis in disease (Salvador, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Salvador, 2010.

claim: Dysfunctional proteasome activity occupies a central position in many neurodegenerative diseases.
source: Dysfunctional proteasome activity occupies a central position in many neurodegenerative diseases, and increased phosphorylation in eIF2α has been detected in postmortem brains of AD patients (Chang et al., 2002).
evidence: Established knowledge supported by citation to Chang et al., 2002.

claim: Increased phosphorylation in eIF2α has been detected in postmortem brains of AD patients.
source: Dysfunctional proteasome activity occupies a central position in many neurodegenerative diseases, and increased phosphorylation in eIF2α has been detected in postmortem brains of AD patients (Chang et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chang et al., 2002.

claim: Prion infection inhibits proteasomal activity and increases polyubiquitin levels by 2–3 times.
source: Prion infection also inhibits proteasomal activity and increases polyubiquitin levels by 2–3 times (similar to the levels observed in our conditions of study- see Figure 1D; Kang et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kang et al., 2004 and comparison to Figure 1D.

claim: Reperfusion after ischemic stroke leads to a profound proteasome inhibition in brain tissue.
source: Strikingly, reperfusion after ischemic stroke leads to a profound proteasome inhibition in brain tissue (Hochrainer et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hochrainer et al., 2012.

claim: In hemorrhagic strokes heme is liberated in the brain and causes neuronal toxicity.
source: In addition, in hemorrhagic strokes heme is liberated in the brain (Babu et al., 2012; Prabhakaran and Naidech, 2012) and causes neuronal toxicity.
evidence: Supported by citations to Babu et al., 2012 and Prabhakaran and Naidech, 2012.

claim: The expression of HRI in neurons and its susceptibility to heme regulation should be considered in the realms of neurodegeneration and iron dyshomeostasis.
source: The expression of HRI in neurons and its susceptibility to heme regulation should thus be considered in the realms of neurodegeneration and iron dyshomeostasis.
evidence: Speculative statement based on the findings and their potential implications.

claim: De novo protein synthesis plays an important role in synaptic transmission and plasticity.
source: Many studies have demonstrated that de novo protein synthesis plays an important role in synaptic transmission and plasticity, (Holt et al., 2019; Sutton and Schuman, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Holt et al., 2019 and Sutton and Schuman, 2006.

claim: Protein degradation, mediated by the ubiquitin proteasome system (UPS), plays an important role in regulating synaptic function.
source: In addition, protein degradation, mediated by the ubiquitin proteasome system (UPS), also plays an important role in regulating synaptic function (Bingol and Schuman, 2006; Tai and Schuman, 2008; Ramachandran and Margolis, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bingol and Schuman, 2006; Tai and Schuman, 2008; Ramachandran and Margolis, 2017.

claim: In neurons, proteome regulation occurs in the cell body as well as the dendrites and axons allowing the initiation of proteome remodeling at synapses, far from the cell body.
source: In neurons, proteome regulation occurs in the cell body as well as the dendrites and axons allowing the initiation of proteome remodeling at synapses, far from the cell body (Holt et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Holt et al., 2019.

claim: Alterations in protein synthesis and degradation, particularly via the ubiquitin proteasome system (UPS), have emerged as network hubs in many disease states.
source: The study of proteostasis is particularly important in neurons because alterations in protein synthesis and degradation, particularly via the ubiquitin proteasome system (UPS), have emerged as network hubs in many disease states (Ciechanover and Brundin, 2003; Labbadia and Morimoto, 2015; Tai and Schuman, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ciechanover and Brundin, 2003; Labbadia and Morimoto, 2015; Tai and Schuman, 2008.
